source.title: Towards Robust Learning with Different Label Noise Distributions
source.authors: Diego Ortego; Eric Arazo; Paul Albert; N. O'Connor; Kevin McGuinness

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the paper and supplementary material. Some figure plots are flattened, and their precise plotted values cannot be recovered from the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains CNNs from scratch on image datasets with artificially corrupted labels and analyzes losses, noisy-image memorization, and downstream accuracy. This directly investigates learning with label noise, though it does not reproduce fully random labels.
record.gate_note: The authors cite prior work for the claim that noisy labels can be completely memorized; that cited result is not extracted. Rows below cover the study's own loss comparisons, qualitative memorization examples, downstream accuracy under different noise settings, and linear-probe findings. Figure-only probe values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own clean/noisy loss trajectories under four ImageNet noise distributions, bearing on V6, and ordinary cross-entropy test accuracy across CIFAR corruption levels, bearing on the generalization component of V4. It does not test perfect fitting of completely random labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that noise distributions differ in how readily clean and noisy samples can be separated by loss, that noisy-label memorization often preserves discriminative intermediate representations, and that DRPL performs strongly across the evaluated datasets. Their own results do not establish perfect fitting of completely random labels.
record.recipe_differences: Uses standard CNN training from scratch with SGD and synthetic label corruption, but studies multiple noise distributions and downstream representation utility rather than reproducing the original fully random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise distribution and corruption level change clean/noisy loss separation and method performance. The authors report weaker small-loss discrimination for non-uniform noise and limitations at high non-uniform out-of-distribution noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation maps for selected noisy samples emphasize image regions that help explain their incorrect training labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models can associate selected mislabeled images with visual regions supporting their noisy labels.

fits_no_version.finding: DRPL retains substantial test accuracy under heavy corruption after detecting noisy labels and using semi-supervised training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Detecting and discarding noisy labels can improve classification performance under label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: Intermediate-feature probes show little degradation in most tested conditions, with degradation across blocks at 80% uniform noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Useful intermediate visual representations can survive noisy-label memorization, depending on corruption level and feature depth.

record.problems: The main memorization evidence is qualitative or figure-based. The paper does not report training error alongside the test accuracies in the extracted noise-level tables, and the supplied text does not provide numerical values for the loss plots or linear-probe plots.
record.rows_left_out: Tables II, IV, and supplementary Tables VI–IX contain many additional accuracy results comparing robust-learning methods. Those method-comparison results were left out except for selected Table VI–VII entries because they do not directly report training fit on completely random labels; Figure 3's detection ROC comparisons are also outside the claim versions.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes are not demonstrated.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or convergence time across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-input fitting experiments.

Perfect training fit at each corruption level, the full trajectory through completely random labels, and a chance-level endpoint are not reported. The ordinary cross-entropy results test only generalization degradation over the sampled corruption levels.
No controlled removal of weight decay, dropout, or augmentation testing both random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Figure 1 does not establish eventual complete memorization, explicit times to learn clean versus noisy labels, or learning trajectories for a wholly random-labeled dataset.

missing.what: Ordinary cross-entropy CIFAR-10/100 test-accuracy sweeps, with separate rows for dataset, noise distribution, corruption level, and best versus last epoch. These are relevant baseline results, rather than merely robust-method comparisons. Uniform-noise best accuracies at 0/20/40/60/80% are 93.87/87.75/83.32/75.71/43.69 for CIFAR-10 and 74.59/59.19/51.44/39.05/19.59 for CIFAR-100.
missing.locator: Table IV, CE entries; supplementary Table VIII, CE Best and Last entries

record.verdict_notes: The introductory assertions of complete memorization and clean-pattern-first learning cite the original sources and are not independent results. Figure 2 concerns memorization of changing pseudo-labels and cannot establish fitting of the original random labels. Differences in noise-detection performance do not by themselves challenge V6.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests several synthetic noise distributions and corruption levels, but not a completely random labeling of the entire training set, test error at chance, or the exact original-source settings.

The study reports test accuracy across corruption levels and discusses memorization, but does not report paired training error showing perfect fitting at each level or a complete smooth trajectory from no corruption to all labels corrupted.
The study compares clean and noisy sample losses during training, but does not compare learning of shared real-data patterns against completely random labels over training.
